column4: Do not exchange God's covenant for a small price, because what is with God is better; immediately before 16:96's contrast between perishing human holdings and what remains with God, this identifies one way a final share is sold away.

Between the person with no afterlife share in 2:200 and the earned share in 2:202, this petitioner asks the Lord for good in both the world and the hereafter, preserving both realms rather than choosing only the nearer one.
God appoints heirs for what parents and relatives leave and commands that covenant partners be given their share; property succession and a due portion are assigned rather than gambled for.

The concluding inheritance ruling measures sibling shares, including the male's portion relative to two females, and closes that God clarifies so people do not stray; allocation and guidance thus meet.
God produces cultivated goods and commands that their due be given on harvest day; the owner receives produce yet must release its share under the Producer's command.
Spend from what God provided before death arrives and the holder asks for delay so he might give charity; retained provision becomes unusable when apparent ownership ends.
Those who hoard gold and silver and do not spend it in God's way turn accumulated property into the cause of painful punishment rather than security.
The hoarded metal of 9:34 is heated and used to brand its owners, who are told to taste what they stored; the kept share becomes the instrument of recompense.
Charitable men and women who lend God a good loan have it multiplied and receive a noble reward; giving property becomes a measured final return from its true owner.
The good loan to God is multiplied many times, while God constricts and expands and to Him people return; the apparent borrower is the one who controls every allotment.
God has purchased believers' lives and wealth in exchange for the Garden; human possession is nested inside a divine transaction whose final payment is the hereafter.
When told to spend from what God provided, disbelievers object that God could feed the needy Himself; their refusal mistakes being entrusted with provision for freedom from the Provider's claim.
God makes people successors on earth, raises some in degrees, and tests them through what He gave; delegated possession and unequal portions are explicitly a trial.
The ayah joins God's creating and forming people, providing good things, and being their Lord; the creator, provider, and owner functions gathered by the source belong to one speaker.
Abraham identifies his Lord as the one who created him and therefore guides him; creation and guidance are one Lord's acts, as 92:3, 92:12, and 92:20 imply.
Everything in the heavens and earth belongs to God, who is the Most High and Great; ownership and divine height meet without the gaming image's “highest” arrow.
The Throne Verse says that whatever is in the heavens and earth belongs to God and ends by naming Him the Most High; possession and height are attributes of the owner.
Dominion is in God's hand and He has power over everything, a compact statement of the true ownership that governs every human portion.
The ayah asks who could provide if God withheld His provision; a person's held wealth depends on a continuing allotment that its holder cannot command.

Qarun says his wealth was given because of knowledge he possesses, but the ayah recalls people God destroyed who were stronger and greater in accumulation; “given” property cannot establish independent ownership.
People desiring worldly life wish for Qarun's like and call him one of great fortune; حَظّ is precisely the apparent lucky share that the passage will overturn.
People of knowledge answer the wishers in 28:79 that God's reward is better for believers who act rightly, moving value from Qarun's visible portion to the final one.
God causes the earth to swallow Qarun and his home, and neither his party nor he can help him; possessed wealth and social power fail at the owner's literal fall.

Those who had wished for Qarun's place recognize that God expands and restricts provision and could have swallowed them too; the scene ends by identifying the allocator behind the fortune they envied.
The garden owner boasts that he has more wealth and a stronger company; his possessive comparison begins a scene that tests whether abundance makes him master.
His companion answers the boast by invoking the one who created him from dust and a drop and fashioned him as a man; creaturely origin corrects the owner's claim.

The owner should have entered his garden saying that it is what God willed and that power belongs only to God, even while seeing his companion as poorer in wealth; possession requires acknowledgment of its source.
The garden's fruit is destroyed and its owner regrets what he spent on it and associating partners with his Lord; “his” property vanishes under the Lord's prior claim.
No group can help the garden owner apart from God, and he cannot save himself; this distinguishes social possession from the power that actually preserves it.
At that point authority belongs to God, the Real, who is best in reward and outcome; the ruined-property scene resolves in true ownership and final recompense.
All have degrees according to what they did so that God may pay their deeds in full without wrong; final rank is an exact earned allotment rather than chance.
Success belongs to the one who purifies the soul; this states the result of the self-purification sought through giving in 92:18.
Failure belongs to the one who corrupts or buries the soul, completing 91:9 with the opposite outcome to purification.
Prosperity belongs to the one who purifies himself, an exact parallel to the giver who offers wealth in order to purify himself.
Whoever purifies himself does so for his own benefit, and the destination is to God; it explains why the giver's purification does not create a debt in the recipient.
The believer who acts rightly receives the best reward and an easy command; moral action, recompense, and yusr meet without any gaming allotment.
God favors some over others in provision, yet the favored resist making those they possess equal partners in it; the ayah exposes selective human claims while asking whether God's favor is denied.
A parable asks whether human owners make those they possess equal partners in the provision God gave them; it uses their own property instincts to clarify exclusive divine ownership.
People fail to measure God according to His true measure, while the whole earth is in His grasp and the heavens folded in His hand; human measures and holdings are dwarfed by the Owner's scale.
Those who desire worldly life and its adornment are paid their deeds there in full; a nearer portion can be completely allotted while still excluding the last.
The people described in 11:15 have nothing in the hereafter but fire, so full worldly payment proves no final share.
Whoever desires the world's reward is given from it, and whoever desires the hereafter's reward is given from it; God, rather than the desirer, dispenses each return.
The believer who does righteous acts, male or female, enters the Garden without even a speck of injustice; this continues 4:123 by joining the created pair to an accurately earned outcome.
Whoever wants worldly reward is reminded that with God are the rewards of both world and hereafter; both possible portions remain at one source.
God expands and restricts provision, while people rejoice in worldly life though it is only slight enjoyment beside the hereafter; size of present allotment and final value are separated.
Give the relative, poor person, and traveler their due and do not squander; property held by one person already contains apportioned claims of others.
The command neither to keep one's hand chained nor extend it completely sets a measured boundary for giving instead of leaving distribution to impulse.
The Lord expands and restricts provision for whom He wills; following the spending boundary in 17:29, this identifies who measures the giver's own resources.
The silver and gold furnishings described in 43:33–34 are only worldly enjoyment, while the hereafter with the Lord is for the reverent; lavish possession is reduced to a temporary share.
Worldly life is play and amusement, whereas belief and reverence bring reward, and God does not ask people for all their wealth; moral ease and recompense do not arise from the world's game.
If God pressed people for their wealth, they would withhold and their resentments would emerge; this directly prepares the call to spend and the exposure of stinginess in 47:38.
God created people from male and female, then made peoples and tribes, but honor with God rests on reverence; created distinctions do not allot final rank by lineage or fortune.
God created the two mates, male and female, an exact repeated formulation of the created pair in 92:3.
The Lord created, proportioned, and balanced the human being; creation is an act of fitting and measure, not an unmeasured cut.
In whatever form God willed He assembled the person, continuing 82:7's measured formation and locating the final shape in divine choice.
After the correction about measured provision and failure to feed the poor, people consume inheritance voraciously; inherited property becomes an unjustly swallowed share.
The passage closes by naming an excessive love of wealth, explaining the possessive instinct behind the misreading and withholding in 89:15–19.
Wealth and children are a trial, while the great reward is with God; apparent possessions test their holder rather than certify his allotted worth.
Wealth and children are only a trial, and with God is a great reward; the repeated formulation separates the held share from the final one.
Believers are warned not to let wealth and children distract them from God's remembrance, since those who do so are the losers; possession can produce loss rather than ease.
Worldly life is called play and amusement, while the hereafter is better for the reverent; it places the source's game inside a wider contrast between temporary play and final value.
Worldly life is only amusement and play, whereas the hereafter is the true life; the gaming scene becomes an emblem of a portion that cannot last.
The Prophet is told not to admire their wealth and children because God may punish them through those very possessions in worldly life; a large share can be an instrument of loss.
This repeated warning again says not to admire wealth and children, through which their owners may be punished before dying unbelieving; possession reverses into burden.
People love the immediate world and leave behind a heavy day; the verse identifies the preference that sacrifices the final portion for the first.
God intends ease and does not intend hardship in the fasting ruling; this is the ordinary y-s-r sense that the source sets beside the root's secondary gambling sense.
Heaped gold and silver and other desired possessions are described as worldly enjoyment, while the best return is with God; visible property is set against what is held at the true destination.
God makes His word the highest; this provides a Quranic “highest” whose value comes from divine truth rather than being the most valuable arrow in a case.
The highest attribute belongs to God, while the evil description belongs to those who deny the hereafter; “highest” is removed from material rank and attached to its owner.
God originates creation and repeats it, and His is the highest attribute in the heavens and earth; creation and divine height meet in one claim.
The ayah asks whether people know that God expands and restricts provision for whom He wills; it is another explicit formulation of the measured worldly share.
The keys of heavens and earth belong to God, who expands and restricts provision; ownership of the stores and allotment from them are joined.

God could give disbelievers silver roofs and stairways if that would not make humanity one unbelieving community; the hypothetical shows how little a lavish worldly allotment signifies, leading to 43:35.
Silver doors and couches continue the hypothetical property display of 43:33, whose status as mere worldly enjoyment is stated in 43:35.
A good loan to God is multiplied and forgiven; the property given returns by a divinely measured increase, though the loan metaphor is broader than the source's lot scene.

The ayah binds each person's “bird” to his neck and brings out his record at resurrection; if ṭāʾir is heard as fortune, it relocates fate from an external omen or lot to the person's disclosed account.
